knowledgeUnits.heading: Coding with context-sensitive prompts

leadVisual.title: What a coding prompt can show

coreExplanation: An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) brings programming tools into one working environment. While code is entered, context-sensitive prompts suggest suitable identifiers, keywords, members or parameters based on the current position and language context.

A prompt can reduce typing and help a programmer recall a routine's interface. The programmer must still select the intended operation and supply meaningful arguments; a syntactically available suggestion may be inappropriate for the problem.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Dynamic syntax checking

leadVisual.title: From a highlight to a correction

coreExplanation: Dynamic syntax checking examines source as it is entered and highlights violations of the language's rules, such as an incomplete expression or a missing keyword. Feedback before a full run helps the programmer locate and correct an error early.

An inline diagnostic can describe the detected problem and indicate its source location. Read the message with the surrounding statement to investigate its cause. A reported location can be where a problem becomes detectable rather than where the original mistake was made.

Syntax checking does not establish that the program solves its intended task. For example, a legal subtraction can still be wrong when the specification requires addition, so expected results and execution evidence are also needed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Pretty-printing and code folding
coreExplanation: Pretty-printing presents source in a consistent readable form, for example by indenting nested blocks and applying syntax colouring to keywords or other language elements. This helps a programmer recognise structure and spot suspicious formatting or missing elements.

Expanding and collapsing code blocks reveals or hides sections in the editor so attention can be focused on the relevant part of a large program. Folding changes the display only: hidden statements still belong to the program and execute whenever control flow reaches them.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Single stepping, breakpoints and inspection
coreExplanation: Single stepping advances through execution one statement at a time, pausing so its effect can be examined before the next statement runs. This lets the programmer relate a change in program state to the instruction that just executed.

A breakpoint pauses execution when a selected location is reached, normally before that statement executes. Place it where relevant values are available and just before the suspect calculation or decision. Reaching a breakpoint does not itself correct the fault.

While paused, variable or expression inspection shows current values for comparison with the expected state. A report window displays information such as program output, run-time errors and diagnostic messages. Its output can be compared with the expected result after stepping an OUTPUT statement; inspecting a variable alone does not execute that output.

Use a deliberate loop of predict, execute one step, inspect and compare. If a watched value changes unexpectedly, inspect the statement that just executed and its inputs rather than placing unrelated breakpoints throughout the program.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Security, privacy and integrity
coreExplanation: Data security protects information against unauthorised access, loss or damage. Privacy concerns the appropriate collection, use and disclosure of personal information. Data integrity concerns accuracy, completeness and consistency, including avoiding incorrect changes during processing or transfer.

These concepts can be affected separately. Restricting access does not make an incorrect value true, and copying a record perfectly does not make its disclosure appropriate. Identify the property affected from what happened to the data, not simply from the presence of a password.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Protect the data and its processing system
coreExplanation: A system must remain available to authorised users and must execute trusted operations. Malware, stolen credentials or damaged hardware can disrupt processing or expose data even when a separate file copy has been protected.

Data also needs protection wherever copies are stored or transferred. A secured computer cannot prevent disclosure from an unencrypted removable drive that has already been lost. Combine system controls with protection of the data and recoverable copies.

knowledgeUnits.heading: User accounts and passwords
coreExplanation: A user account gives a person a distinct identity on a computer or network. The system associates that identity with permissions and an activity record. Separate accounts help attribute actions to individual users.

A password is secret knowledge used to authenticate the claimed identity. The system checks the supplied password against the account's stored verifier before accepting the login. Hard-to-guess passwords and limits on repeated attempts reduce guessing; a disclosed password can still be misused.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Create and verify a digital signature
coreExplanation: The sender applies a hash algorithm to a message to produce a digest, then signs that digest using the sender's private key. In the simplified signing model, this is described as encrypting the digest. The sender sends the message together with the digital signature.

The receiver uses the sender's public key to verify the signature; in the simplified model, decrypting the signature recovers the sender's digest. The receiver also hashes the received message with the same algorithm and compares the digests. A match supports the claimed origin and shows that the signed content has not changed, provided the public key is correctly associated with the sender.

A digital signature does not make the message unreadable. Confidentiality requires encryption separately. Signing the digest must not be confused with sending the private key or merely appending an unprotected checksum.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Biometric authentication
coreExplanation: Biometrics use a physical or behavioural feature, such as a fingerprint, iris, voice or typing pattern. A sensor captures the feature and software extracts a template that is compared with an enrolled reference.

A sufficient match authenticates the identity claim. False acceptance can admit an impostor, while false rejection can deny a legitimate user. Sensors and protected templates are needed, and a compromised biological feature cannot be replaced as easily as a password.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Firewalls on a PC and at a network boundary
coreExplanation: A firewall checks incoming and outgoing traffic against configured rules, for example rules about addresses, ports, protocols or connection state. It allows permitted traffic and blocks disallowed traffic; it may also log decisions.

A host firewall runs on one computer. A network firewall filters traffic passing through a network boundary. Neither arrangement guarantees that all harmful content is detected: permitted traffic can still carry a deceptive message or malicious download, and poorly chosen rules can leave unwanted access open.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Anti-virus software
coreExplanation: Anti-virus software scans files, memory or activity for known virus signatures and suspicious behaviour. On detection it can block execution, isolate a file in quarantine, or remove the malicious code.

Detection information must be updated as new threats are identified. Quarantine prevents normal use of a suspicious file while preserving it for review. New or concealed malware may escape detection, so a successful scan does not prove that every file is safe.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Anti-spyware software
coreExplanation: Anti-spyware looks for software that covertly monitors activity or collects information. It can detect a monitoring component, stop it, quarantine it or remove it. Detection may be included within a broader anti-malware product.

Removing spyware reduces further collection but cannot retrieve information already sent to a third party. Exposed credentials may need replacing, and the entry route should be addressed to reduce reinfection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine controls for different risks
coreExplanation: Encryption changes readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. It protects the confidentiality of stored or intercepted copies; the authorised application needs the correct key to recover readable data.

Choose controls by mechanism. Login authentication checks identity, a firewall filters connections, anti-malware addresses malicious software, and encryption protects content outside normal access paths. Combining these controls reduces different risks without assuming that any one control replaces the others.

objectives.description: Explain how spyware collects and discloses information.

Select and describe precautions whose mechanisms restrict a stated threat.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Viruses attach to a host and replicate
coreExplanation: A virus is malicious code that attaches to or modifies a host file or program. Running the infected host can execute the virus and allow it to replicate into further files. Its payload may corrupt information, delete data or disrupt the computer.

Networks, shared files and downloaded attachments provide routes for infected hosts to reach other computers. Avoid executing untrusted files and use maintained detection software to reduce this risk.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Spyware monitors and discloses
coreExplanation: Spyware covertly monitors activity or collects data, for example by logging keystrokes or recording the screen. Collected information may be sent to a third party, exposing private details or credentials.

Its defining feature is covert collection, not necessarily self-replication. Anti-spyware can address the installed component, while controlled installation and caution with downloads reduce entry opportunities.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Unauthorised access by hackers
coreExplanation: In this security context, a hacker gains or attempts unauthorised access to a system or its data. Weak credentials, exposed services or unpatched vulnerabilities can provide an entry route.

The resulting access may permit disclosure, alteration or disruption. Strong authentication reduces impersonation, software patches address known vulnerabilities, and access rights limit what a compromised account can do.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Phishing persuades the user
coreExplanation: A phishing message impersonates a trusted organisation or person and persuades the recipient to disclose information or perform an unsafe action. It may use urgency and a link to a fake sign-in page to capture credentials.

Check the request through an independently obtained contact or known website rather than the message's link. Filtering and training reduce exposure; multi-factor authentication can reduce the impact of a stolen password but does not make every deceptive request harmless.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Pharming changes the destination
coreExplanation: Pharming redirects a user to a fraudulent site, for example by corrupting DNS or local name-resolution information. The user may type the intended address correctly yet be directed to a different destination.

Protect name-resolution settings, update affected software and investigate certificate or hostname warnings. An HTTPS indicator alone does not prove that a site is legitimate; examine the intended destination and do not ignore a certificate mismatch.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match precautions to the threat
coreExplanation: A useful precaution interrupts a specific route or reduces a specific consequence. Explain that link: patching repairs a known software weakness, permission restrictions reduce exposure, and independent verification challenges a deceptive request.

Controls reduce risk rather than eliminate every possible incident. Combining prevention, detection and recovery allows a response when one measure fails. Choose controls appropriate to the system and explain what remains outside each control's role.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Encryption and decryption

leadVisual.title: From readable data to a protected copy

coreExplanation: Encryption applies an algorithm and key to plaintext, producing ciphertext. Decryption applies the corresponding algorithm and correct key to recover the original readable information. An intercepted or stolen encrypted copy should be unintelligible to someone without the required key.

Protect the key separately from the encrypted copy. Encryption does not decide which logged-in user may edit a record, prevent deletion of ciphertext, or prove that the source data was true. Its main role here is confidentiality.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Apply access rights to data
coreExplanation: Access rights associate users or roles with permitted actions on a resource. Read permits viewing, modify permits alteration, and delete permits removal. A service checks the requested operation against these permissions after identifying the user.

Least privilege gives a role only the rights needed for its work. Restricting read access supports confidentiality; restricting changes supports integrity. Rights on a server do not protect an unencrypted copy outside that server, and authorised users can still make mistakes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Validation and verification answer different questions

leadVisual.title: A source mark of 46 is entered as 64

coreExplanation: Validation tests whether input satisfies stated rules and is reasonable for its purpose. Verification checks whether information has been entered, copied or transferred accurately relative to its source. Both reduce the acceptance of errors and so help maintain data integrity.

A plausible wrong value can pass validation, and two copies of a false original can agree. Neither process proves that the source is true. Use both when a system needs acceptable values and faithful copying.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Range and limit checks
coreExplanation: A range check applies both a lower and an upper bound, such as 0 <= Mark <= 75. Test both endpoints as well as values outside them; the stated rule decides whether the bounds are inclusive.

A limit check applies one upper or lower bound, such as FileSize <= 10 MiB. It does not introduce a second bound that was not specified. Choose a range when both ends matter and a limit when the requirement supplies one bound.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Format and length checks

leadVisual.title: Code rule: two uppercase letters, then four digits

coreExplanation: A format check tests a required pattern, for example two uppercase letters followed by four digits. A length check tests the number of characters, for example exactly six. The two checks ask different questions about the same string.
A six-character value can still have the wrong format. Check the complete pattern and the specified character count, preserving leading zeros when a code is a string.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Presence and existence checks

leadVisual.title: Stored customer IDs: C102, C107, C115

coreExplanation: A presence check requires an entry rather than a blank required field. An existence check looks for the supplied value in a specified stored lookup or file, such as checking that a customer identifier belongs to an existing customer.
A value can be present but absent from the lookup. Define which field is required and which stored set supplies valid identifiers; do not confuse these checks with a format test.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate and check an identifier's check digit

leadVisual.title: Weighted check digit: a complete calculation

coreExplanation: A check digit is derived from the other digits in an identifier and stored with them. On entry or scanning, the system repeats the stated calculation and compares the expected check digit with the supplied digit. A mismatch causes rejection or re-entry.

Use the algorithm given in the question: different schemes use different weights and moduli. For the example here, multiply the four data digits by 3, 1, 3, 1 and choose a final digit that makes the total a multiple of 10. Some errors can still produce the same check digit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Verify entered data
coreExplanation: For a visual check, a person compares the entered value with the original source and investigates differences. It is a comparison with a source, not simply a judgement that the value looks reasonable.

For double entry, the value is entered independently twice and the computer compares the entries. A mismatch is flagged for correction or re-entry. Agreement still cannot establish that the original source is correct, and repeating the same mistake can evade detection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use parity on a byte
coreExplanation: A parity bit is chosen so the total number of 1 bits, including that bit, has the agreed even or odd parity. The examples use seven data bits and one parity bit to form an eight-bit transmitted group.

The receiver counts the 1s and compares the result with the agreed convention. Any odd number of flipped bits changes parity and is detected. An even number of flips can leave parity unchanged; the check alone cannot identify the incorrect bit or prove the byte is correct.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use row and column parity

leadVisual.title: Locate a single-bit error by intersection

coreExplanation: Block parity organises transmitted groups into rows, applies a parity bit to each row, and adds a parity row or byte for the columns. The receiver checks parity in both directions using the agreed convention.

If exactly one bit has changed, the failing row and failing column intersect at that bit, allowing it to be located and corrected by flipping it. Multiple errors may be ambiguous or undetected; four flipped corner bits in a rectangle leave every affected row and column parity unchanged.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate and compare a checksum
coreExplanation: The sender calculates a value from a data block using an agreed checksum algorithm and sends it with the data. The receiver applies the same algorithm to the received block and compares its result with the transmitted checksum.

A mismatch indicates an error and can trigger rejection or retransmission. A match means no error was detected by that checksum; different data can produce the same value. Use the stated algorithm rather than assuming that all checksums are simple sums.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why computing professionals need ethics

leadVisual.title: From specialist knowledge to an informed decision

coreExplanation: Ethics concerns principles about right and wrong conduct. A computing professional makes decisions that can affect other people's safety, privacy, opportunities and resources. Users may lack the technical knowledge or access needed to detect an unsafe system or challenge its design, so technical power brings responsibilities.

Professional ethics helps guide decisions when interests conflict or a rule does not settle what should be done. Its purposes include protecting the public interest, promoting honest and competent work, maintaining trust and making professionals accountable for foreseeable effects of their decisions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Professional duties and legal compliance
coreExplanation: A professional should work within their competence, report limitations honestly, protect confidential information and consider effects on the public. Conflicting interests should be disclosed so that advice can be evaluated fairly. For example, a paid relationship with a supplier can influence a recommendation even when that recommendation is technically possible.

Law sets enforceable requirements; ethical judgement also considers what is responsible in the particular circumstances. An employer's instruction or the absence of an explicit legal prohibition does not remove a professional's duty to consider harm. A defensible response records the concern, seeks appropriate guidance and proposes an action that addresses it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: BCS, IEEE and the value of membership
coreExplanation: BCS is the British Computer Society. IEEE is the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. These professional bodies provide codes of conduct or ethics that express standards expected of members. A shared code gives a practitioner a reference when explaining a professional concern to an employer or client.

Joining can provide continuing professional development, technical information and contact with experienced peers. These help members maintain competence and obtain guidance when a problem exceeds their experience. Membership also brings expectations of conduct and accountability through the body's professional processes, supporting public confidence in the profession.

A code supports judgement but cannot guarantee that every member acts ethically. Membership does not replace the law, remove personal responsibility or automatically certify every product a member develops.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Identify the decision and the people affected
coreExplanation: Begin with the actual decision: what is someone proposing to collect, disclose, change or conceal? Identify direct stakeholders, such as users and employees, and others affected indirectly, such as families or the wider public. Different groups may have different interests in the same system.

Connect each stakeholder to a relevant responsibility. A school handling location data has duties towards pupils' privacy as well as safety. Naming 'society' without explaining a connection is too vague to support a judgement. Benefits and harms are parallel possibilities to investigate; one is not automatically the cause of the other.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare ethical and unethical actions

leadVisual.title: Compare the consequences of two actions

coreExplanation: Explain consequences through a cause-and-effect link: the action changes what happens to a stakeholder. For example, disclosing a known defect allows a client to avoid relying on unsafe output; concealing it can lead the client to make a harmful decision with misplaced confidence.

Consider both courses of action. Acting ethically can have an immediate cost, such as delay or extra testing, while preserving safety and trust. Acting unethically may produce a short-term advantage but can cause harm, complaints, loss of confidence or professional consequences. State consequences supported by the situation rather than assuming that every outcome is certain.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Justify a proportionate response
coreExplanation: Use evidence to weigh the stated purpose against the effects on people. Compare a realistic alternative that could meet the purpose with less intrusion or risk. Proportionality means the action should be appropriate to the need and no more intrusive or harmful than necessary to achieve it.

A conclusion should identify an action and explain why it is justified. Relevant safeguards might include limiting collection and retention, restricting access, correcting inaccurate information or providing a way to challenge a decision. A safeguard needs a mechanism linked to the particular risk, and it may reduce rather than eliminate that risk.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why software needs copyright protection

leadVisual.title: Ownership and permission perform different roles

coreExplanation: Writing software takes time, skill and investment, while copying a finished program can cost very little. Copyright legislation gives the rights holder enforceable control over protected expression such as original source code and documentation. This allows unauthorised copying or distribution to be challenged and enables creators to grant permissions and obtain revenue from their work.

Copyright protects the expression of a program rather than every underlying idea or mathematical method. A licence grants permission for specified acts under conditions; buying a copy normally does not transfer ownership of its copyright. A user should establish the applicable permissions before copying, modifying or redistributing software, taking account of any relevant legal exceptions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Free software and the Free Software Foundation
coreExplanation: The Free Software Foundation (FSF) promotes software freedom. Its approach gives users freedoms to run a program for any purpose, study and change it, redistribute copies, and distribute modified versions. Access to source code is necessary for studying how the program works and making useful changes.

Free refers to these freedoms, not necessarily a zero price. A copy or support service can be sold while the user retains the freedoms granted by a free-software licence. Some licences use copyleft conditions to preserve freedoms in distributed derivatives; not every free-software licence imposes the same redistribution conditions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Open source and the Open Source Initiative

leadVisual.title: Check rights as well as source access

coreExplanation: The Open Source Initiative (OSI) maintains the Open Source Definition and approves licences that satisfy its criteria. Open-source licensing includes access to source code and permission to modify and redistribute the software. Merely allowing users to look at source code is insufficient if the licence prohibits the necessary uses or redistribution.

FSF and OSI are organisations, not two individual licences. Many licences satisfy both free-software and open-source criteria. Their emphasis differs: the FSF stresses users' freedoms, while the OSI evaluates licences against open-source criteria. For a real choice, read the licence's obligations, such as keeping notices or conditions on distributing modified work.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Shareware: evaluate before continued use

leadVisual.title: A trial has terms and a continuation decision

coreExplanation: Shareware is distributed so users can try software before paying for continued or complete use. A trial may expire after a stated period or restrict features until a licence is purchased. The exact trial terms determine what use and copying are permitted.

This approach can reduce the risk of buying an unsuitable program because a user can test it on their own system. However, a successful trial is not a permanent entitlement, and shareware does not automatically include source code or permission to modify it. Budget for any required payment and check what happens when the trial ends.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Commercial and proprietary software

leadVisual.title: Separate user permissions from the price of a copy

coreExplanation: Commercial software is developed or supplied as a business activity. A supplier may earn income from licences, subscriptions, support or other services. Commercial and proprietary are not synonyms: a business can sell free or open-source software, while proprietary software can sometimes be offered without payment.

A proprietary licence commonly permits specified use while limiting copying, modification or redistribution. Terms may specify the number of users or devices, duration and support arrangements. Paid support can be useful when it is actually included in the agreement; payment alone does not guarantee support, source access or unrestricted installation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose a licence from the requirements

leadVisual.title: Match a requirement to a licence feature

coreExplanation: Identify the organisation's required acts before selecting software: running it on the intended devices, modifying source, distributing copies or obtaining support. Then compare those needs with the permissions, costs and obligations of the offered licences. A cheap option is unsuitable if its terms prohibit a required act.

A justification connects a stated requirement to a licence feature and its consequence. Check practical limits as well: source modification needs skilled staff, a trial needs a continuation plan, and supplier support needs agreed scope and availability. There is no single licence category that is best for every organisation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: What artificial intelligence does
coreExplanation: Artificial intelligence (AI) enables computer systems to perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as interpreting language, recognising patterns, reasoning or making predictions and decisions. A system may use expert-written rules or a model learned from data to infer an output for a new input.

An AI system does not have to be a physical robot, conscious or human-like in every respect. A recommendation service can use AI entirely in software. Conversely, recording information or performing a fixed arithmetic calculation does not by itself demonstrate AI. Identify the interpretation, inference or decision task being performed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: From input to an AI-assisted action

leadVisual.title: Follow a maintenance prediction from input to use

coreExplanation: Describe an application as a connected chain. State the input information, what the AI infers or recognises, the resulting output and how that output is used. 'AI is used in medicine' names an area but does not explain an application; interpreting a scan to flag a possible abnormality gives a task and a use.

Outputs can guide a person or control an action. A fraud-detection model may flag a payment for an investigator, while an autonomous controller may select an action from sensor readings. Confidence, reliability and consequences determine how much checking or human intervention is appropriate. A prediction can be useful without being certain.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Social effects: access, fairness and privacy

leadVisual.title: Look beyond an overall accuracy figure

coreExplanation: Social impacts concern how people live, participate and are treated. Speech recognition can improve access for someone unable to type, and translation can help people communicate. The benefit depends on whether the system works adequately for its users, including different accents, languages or disabilities.

Biased or unrepresentative data can contribute to unequal error rates and unfair decisions. Collecting personal information also creates privacy risks. Explain who benefits or is harmed: a hiring system that rejects qualified applicants unfairly changes their opportunities. Testing across affected groups, limiting unnecessary collection and providing human review or appeal can reduce specific risks.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Economic effects: productivity, work and cost

leadVisual.title: Account for more than one cost

coreExplanation: Economic impacts concern resources, production, costs and employment. An AI tool may process routine cases more quickly, reduce waste or predict failures before expensive disruption. Link the saving to the activity: an early equipment warning may allow planned maintenance during a quiet period rather than an emergency shutdown.

Costs include developing or buying the system, obtaining and maintaining suitable data, operating hardware and training staff. Incorrect decisions can create rework or losses. Automation may reduce demand for some tasks while creating or changing roles in supervision, maintenance and specialist support; workers may need retraining. A productivity gain does not mean every worker or business benefits equally.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Environmental costs and potential savings

leadVisual.title: Compare application savings with the system footprint

coreExplanation: Training and operating AI models uses computing equipment and electricity, and cooling may require water or additional energy. Manufacturing and replacing hardware also uses materials and produces waste. Emissions depend partly on the energy supply, so identical computation can have different environmental consequences in different settings.

An AI application can also reduce resource use: optimising delivery routes may reduce fuel consumption, adjusting heating to occupancy may reduce energy waste, and detecting faults may prolong equipment life. Compare these savings with the system's own operation and hardware lifecycle. The result depends on the scale of use and the alternative being replaced, not on an assumption that all AI is environmentally beneficial or harmful.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Evaluate an application in its setting
coreExplanation: Start an evaluation by identifying the AI task and the decision it influences. Develop relevant benefits and drawbacks through effects on named stakeholders or resources. Consider social, economic and environmental dimensions where they apply to the question, but do not force an unrelated point into a response simply to repeat three labels.

Reach a supported judgement using the supplied constraints. State a suitable safeguard or alternative and explain the risk it addresses. Human oversight needs a workable review process and competent reviewers; writing 'a human checks it' does not establish that errors will be caught. A conditional recommendation should say which evidence or conditions would make deployment acceptable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: From repeated facts to linked tables
coreExplanation: A file-based approach keeps data in files managed by individual applications. Repeating a patient's address in appointment and billing files uses extra storage. If only the billing copy is updated, the two applications may report different addresses for the same patient.

A relational design can store the address in Patient and put PatientID in related records. Applications retrieve the shared fact through that relationship. Central queries, constraints and access controls also reduce isolated retrieval and duplicated control code; the benefits depend on the design and its enforcement.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Entities, tables, records and fields

leadVisual.title: From an entity to its stored representation

coreExplanation: An entity is a type of real-world object or concept about which data is stored, such as Patient. A table represents occurrences of that entity. One row is a record, also called a tuple; it describes one particular patient.

An attribute is a named property of the entity, such as PatientName. A field is the corresponding column in its table. Distinguish the property from one value: PatientName is the field, while 'Imani' is a value in a particular record.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose keys for identification and retrieval
coreExplanation: A candidate key is a minimal field or combination of fields that uniquely identifies a record. One candidate is selected as the primary key; its values must be unique and not null. A composite key uses more than one field, with every component needed for uniqueness.

A secondary key provides an additional way to retrieve records, such as looking up all patients in one town; it need not be unique. A foreign key stores a reference to a key in a related table. The same patient can therefore appear as the foreign-key value in several appointments.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read relationship cardinality in both directions

leadVisual.title: Read each relationship in both directions

coreExplanation: Relationship cardinality describes how many occurrences on one side may be associated with an occurrence on the other. Read the business rule in both directions before choosing one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.

If a student can join several clubs and a club can have several students, the relationship is many-to-many. A Membership table records each student-club association and gives two one-to-many relationships. The pair of identifiers can be its composite key when each membership occurs only once.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Prevent references to missing records

leadVisual.title: A reference must reach an existing record

coreExplanation: Referential integrity requires each non-null foreign-key value to match an existing referenced key value. If an appointment names PatientID 99 but no such patient exists, a declared foreign-key constraint can reject that appointment.

Updates and deletions must also preserve valid links. Deleting a referenced patient can be rejected, or handled by an explicitly defined referential action. A nullable foreign key may be null where the design allows no association; it must not hold an arbitrary unmatched identifier.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use an index to find matching records

leadVisual.title: An index provides another access path

coreExplanation: An index is an additional lookup structure associated with one or more fields. It relates indexed values to record locations so the DBMS can find matches without inspecting every table row in suitable queries.

An index on Town can help retrieve all patients in York even when Town is not unique. The index occupies storage and must be maintained when indexed data changes. It improves an access path; it does not replace the table or guarantee that stored facts are correct.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Document entities, keys and relationship cardinality
coreExplanation: Extract entity types from the facts that the organisation needs to store, then identify each entity's key and relevant attributes. Connect entities only when the business rules support an association. An E-R diagram records this structure rather than a sequence of processing steps.

In this clinic, each appointment involves exactly one patient and one doctor. A patient or doctor may have many appointments. Appointment therefore stores both foreign keys, and its separate AppointmentID allows the same patient to visit the same doctor on different occasions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: 1NF: one value in each field
coreExplanation: First Normal Form requires atomic field values and no repeating groups. For this ordering system, a list of product entries in one order field is a repeating group. Give each product line its own row while retaining the order and customer information needed to interpret that row.

Assume each product occurs at most once per order and the stored unit price is the product's current fixed price. The pair (OrderID, ProductID) identifies a line. Separating the list makes values atomic, but repeated customer and product details still remain to be addressed in later normal forms.

knowledgeUnits.heading: 2NF: depend on the whole composite key

leadVisual.title: 2NF: separate facts with a partial dependency

coreExplanation: Second Normal Form requires 1NF and no partial dependency of a non-key attribute on part of a candidate key. In the order example, ProductName and UnitPrice depend on ProductID alone, while CustomerID and CustomerName depend on OrderID alone. Quantity depends on the whole line key.

Move the product facts to Product and the order-level facts to SalesOrder. Keep OrderLine for the association and quantity, retaining the two identifying fields as references. This decomposition removes partial dependencies but does not yet separate CustomerName from CustomerID inside SalesOrder.

knowledgeUnits.heading: 3NF: remove transitive dependencies
coreExplanation: Third Normal Form requires 2NF and, in these simple designs, no dependency of one non-key attribute on another non-key attribute. SalesOrder still contains OrderID determining CustomerID and CustomerID determining CustomerName. The customer's name is transitively dependent on the order identifier.

Create Customer(CustomerID, CustomerName) and retain CustomerID as a foreign key in SalesOrder. Customer facts can then be updated in their own relation. Product and OrderLine remain unchanged; the existing keys allow the original order information to be reconstructed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Judge and produce a complete 3NF design

leadVisual.title: Check that the original facts remain recoverable

coreExplanation: To judge a design, name its key, state the relevant dependencies and test each normal form in order. One row per entity is not sufficient evidence of 3NF. A non-key fact can still describe another entity, producing an update, insertion or deletion anomaly.

To produce a design, assign each fact to its determinant and explicitly retain primary and foreign keys. Check that every original attribute is accounted for and that a representative original record can be reconstructed. State any assumptions about uniqueness instead of inventing extra dependencies.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Data management and the data dictionary
coreExplanation: A DBMS provides software services to store, retrieve and update database data. It maintains a data dictionary containing metadata: information about the database's tables, fields, types, lengths, keys and constraints rather than the ordinary records themselves.

When a table or query is defined, the DBMS can consult that metadata to check field names and permitted structures. Maintaining definitions centrally reduces the risk that separate applications use conflicting assumptions about the same stored data.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Represent the organisation's data

leadVisual.title: Translate a business rule into a model

coreExplanation: Data modelling identifies the entities, attributes and relationships required by an organisation. It starts from the information and business rules, such as whether one appointment may involve several doctors, rather than from how bytes will be arranged on disk.

A DBMS modelling tool can help create and inspect the relationships before they are implemented as tables. The designer must still confirm that the model matches the stated requirements; software cannot infer every business rule from field names.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define the logical schema
coreExplanation: The logical schema specifies the logical organisation of the database: its tables, attributes, data types, keys, relationships and constraints. Programs can use these definitions without knowing the physical disk locations of individual records.

A model of pupils and groups can become Pupil(PupilID, PupilName, GroupID) and TutorGroup(GroupID, GroupName), with specified primary and foreign keys. The schema is the design being defined; the data dictionary stores metadata describing that design.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Enforce valid values and relationships

leadVisual.title: Check a change before accepting it

coreExplanation: Integrity constraints restrict invalid or inconsistent database changes. A primary key identifies records uniquely, a foreign key checks a declared reference, and field types or validation rules restrict values to a permitted domain.

For an examination database, a rule can require Mark to be between 0 and 100 and CandidateID to refer to an existing candidate. The DBMS rejects changes violating those rules. A plausible but incorrectly transcribed mark can still pass them, so integrity constraints do not establish factual truth.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assign access rights to users and groups

leadVisual.title: Permit operations according to user roles

coreExplanation: Database security restricts who can access stored information and which operations are permitted. After authentication establishes identity, access rights can allow reading selected data while denying insertion, modification or deletion.

Rights may be assigned to an individual account or to a group representing a role. A school can give Tutors access to contact information and the Finance group permission to update fees. Group membership must be maintained when responsibilities change.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Back up and recover a consistent database
coreExplanation: A backup procedure creates a recoverable copy of database state. Schedule backups often enough for the acceptable data-loss interval, protect copies from the same failure as the live system, and restrict access because the copies may contain sensitive records.

Recovery restores a suitable consistent backup after loss or corruption. Where the DBMS supports transaction logs, later recorded changes may be replayed to a chosen recovery point. Periodic restore tests check that the stored copies and procedure actually work.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use the developer interface

leadVisual.title: Build the objects and interfaces users need

coreExplanation: A DBMS developer interface supplies tools for constructing database objects and applications. A developer can define tables and constraints and build forms or reports that use the database without manually implementing every interface component.

For a school admissions form, the developer chooses the fields, configures validation and links controls to the appropriate data. The resulting form collects a new pupil record. Designing that form is distinct from the query processor carrying out its eventual data request.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a query through the query processor

leadVisual.title: Turn a SQL request into a result

coreExplanation: A query processor interprets a submitted query, checks its syntax and references, and determines how to carry out the requested data access. It can use table definitions and available indexes when choosing a suitable execution plan.

It executes the plan and produces the requested result while DBMS permissions and integrity rules apply. A staff query for overdue loans therefore involves locating, filtering and returning records; it does not require rebuilding the data-entry form each time.

knowledgeUnits.heading: DDL changes structure

leadVisual.title: Distinguish a new attribute from a new value

coreExplanation: Data Definition Language defines and modifies database structure. It can create a database, define a table's attributes and constraints, or alter an existing table definition. These operations determine what data the database can store.
Creating a Loan table does not add a particular loan record. Similarly, adding DueDate changes the permitted structure for loan records rather than choosing the date for one member's loan.

knowledgeUnits.heading: DML retrieves and maintains records
coreExplanation: Data Manipulation Language works with records in the defined structure. SELECT retrieves specified information. INSERT INTO adds records, UPDATE changes stored field values, and DELETE FROM removes records.

A query can produce a result table without altering the stored rows. Updating one member's phone number changes data while leaving the Member field definitions intact. These are both DML operations in the syllabus classification.

knowledgeUnits.heading: SQL expresses both kinds of operation

leadVisual.title: SQL includes both DDL and DML

coreExplanation: Structured Query Language (SQL) is the industry-standard language used for both DDL and DML. The DBMS interprets SQL statements and carries out their requested changes or queries. DDL and DML describe roles within SQL rather than two alternative database products.

Determine the category from the requested effect, not from the word 'change' alone. A SQL statement that changes a column's definition is structural; one that changes the current value in that column operates on data.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read the supplied statement before explaining it

leadVisual.title: Read what each SQL clause asks for

coreExplanation: A SQL statement must be interpreted from the actual identifiers, conditions and values supplied. In a retrieval statement, SELECT identifies output expressions, FROM identifies the source and WHERE restricts rows. A changed field list can alter the columns without changing which records qualify.

Read a definition statement by identifying the object created or altered, its field types and its constraints. Quoted text literals represent values rather than field names. Explain the effect of the operator or limit given; recognising a keyword alone does not determine the result.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Create a named database

leadVisual.title: Create the database before defining its tables

coreExplanation: CREATE DATABASE creates a named database in a DBMS that supports this SQL operation. The name is an identifier, not a quoted data value. Creating the database does not by itself define its tables or populate records.

After creating SchoolLibrary, the developer selects that database in the chosen DBMS interface and defines its tables. The interface command for selecting a database varies between products; the SQL statement below expresses the required creation operation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose data types and define fields

leadVisual.title: Choose a type from the meaning of a value

coreExplanation: Choose a field type from the meaning and range of its values. CHARACTER stores fixed-length character data; VARCHAR(n) stores text up to the specified maximum length. INTEGER represents whole numbers, REAL represents values with a fractional part, and BOOLEAN represents true or false.

DATE and TIME represent calendar dates and times of day separately. Field names and types appear inside the CREATE TABLE brackets, separated by commas. A numeric-looking identifier may still need a text type when leading zeroes or non-arithmetic meaning must be preserved.

workedExample.title: Create a referenced table before its child

knowledgeUnits.heading: Alter an existing table definition

leadVisual.title: ALTER TABLE adds a field to the definition

coreExplanation: ALTER TABLE changes the structure of an existing table. To add Email to the Student definition, identify the existing table and supply the new field name and type after ADD. Existing student records remain present.

In this example the added Email field is nullable and has no default, so existing records initially have no supplied email value. Setting an email for one student is a later UPDATE operation. The new attribute and the value in one occurrence are separate changes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare the primary key

leadVisual.title: A primary key identifies each record

coreExplanation: A PRIMARY KEY constraint declares the chosen identifier for a table. The key must distinguish every record and cannot be null. Write the selected field inside PRIMARY KEY brackets in the CREATE TABLE definition.

A composite primary key lists all fields needed for identification, for example PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID) in Membership. The combination must be unique; either component may recur in other combinations. Choose the key from the stated business rules.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare the referenced relationship

leadVisual.title: Declare which field references which key

coreExplanation: FOREIGN KEY names the field or fields in the current table; REFERENCES names the related table and referenced key. In Student, FOREIGN KEY (TutorID) REFERENCES Tutor(TutorID) declares which parent identifier each non-null tutor reference must match.

Create the referenced table and key first when using this teaching sequence. The child field may repeat when many students share a tutor. A foreign-key declaration enforces the link; it does not automatically assign a tutor or create the missing parent record.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose the result columns and source
coreExplanation: SELECT lists the fields or expressions required in the result, while FROM names the source table. Returning MemberName alone does not return MemberID or Active. Reading a result leaves the original Member records unchanged.

Use the Member and Loan data in this lesson to trace each request. Each example states any required ordering explicitly; without ORDER BY, a DBMS need not return records in insertion or primary-key order.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Filter rows using a Boolean condition

leadVisual.title: WHERE: both conditions must be true

coreExplanation: WHERE retains only records for which the condition is true. Combine comparisons with AND when all conditions must hold, or OR when an alternative is sufficient. Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit in compound expressions.
The Loan example requires an unreturned loan and a fee of at least 3. Loan 202 has a sufficient fee but is returned; loan 201 is unreturned but its fee is only 2. Neither satisfies both conditions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Sort the returned records

leadVisual.title: ORDER BY rearranges the result rows

coreExplanation: ORDER BY arranges result rows by the specified field or expression. ASC means increasing order and is the default; DESC means decreasing order. Sorting changes result presentation rather than the stored values.

Multiple sort fields are applied in sequence: sort by the first field, then use the next field for ties. The example sorts fees from largest to smallest and uses LoanID ascending to make any equal-fee ordering predictable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Form groups before calculating group results

leadVisual.title: GROUP BY forms one group per key value

coreExplanation: GROUP BY places records sharing the grouping values into the same group. An aggregate can then calculate one result for each group. Grouping loans by MemberID lets COUNT(*) report the number of loans for each represented member.

Include non-aggregated selected fields in GROUP BY so each returned value has a defined meaning for the group. ORDER BY can subsequently arrange the grouped results; it does not create the groups. A member with no Loan row does not appear in a grouping of Loan alone.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match records from two tables with INNER JOIN

leadVisual.title: INNER JOIN returns matching row pairs

coreExplanation: An INNER JOIN combines row pairs satisfying its ON condition. Here Member.MemberID = Loan.MemberID connects each loan to its member. Qualify shared field names with the table name to make the intended reference unambiguous.

A member with two loans contributes two joined rows, while a member with no matching loan contributes none. WHERE may further filter the joined rows. These AS SQL tasks use at most two tables; use an explicit INNER JOIN and a separate ON matching condition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate SUM, COUNT and AVG

leadVisual.title: Aggregates calculate over the selected records

coreExplanation: SUM adds the numeric values of an expression, COUNT(*) counts records, and AVG calculates the mean of the included non-null values. Without GROUP BY, an aggregate query calculates one overall result for the selected records.

For the five library fees, 2 + 4 + 6 + 0 + 3 = 15, with five records and a mean of 3. A null denotes a missing value: COUNT(Fee), SUM(Fee) and AVG(Fee) ignore null fees, whereas COUNT(*) still counts their rows. Zero is a known numeric value and remains included.

workedExample.title: Calculate the same result by hand

knowledgeUnits.heading: Insert values into named fields

leadVisual.title: INSERT INTO adds a new record

coreExplanation: INSERT INTO adds a record. Name the target fields and supply the corresponding VALUES in the same order. Text literals use single quotes; numeric and Boolean values are written according to their types.

Check the new primary key and any foreign-key values before insertion. The library example adds MemberID 5 with the name Elena and Active TRUE. It does not alter an existing member's record, and it must fail if that primary key is already present.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Delete only the intended records

leadVisual.title: DELETE FROM removes the selected row

coreExplanation: DELETE FROM removes complete records from the named table. WHERE selects the records to remove. To remove the completed loan with LoanID 204, match that identifier rather than a member identifier shared by several loans.

Without a WHERE condition, deletion targets all rows in the table, subject to constraints. Check the intended rows first with a corresponding SELECT. Removing a referenced parent may be rejected by foreign-key constraints; this example removes the child Loan record.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change fields while keeping the record

leadVisual.title: UPDATE changes a field in the selected record

coreExplanation: UPDATE names the table, SET supplies the new field values, and WHERE selects the affected records. Updating Returned to TRUE for LoanID 203 leaves that loan's identity, member and fee in place.

A missing or incorrect WHERE condition can affect unintended records. Decide whether the business task requires changing a value or removing a record, then verify both the affected rows and the values that should remain unchanged.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 1: Information representation
coreExplanation: Show understanding of binary magnitudes and the difference between binary prefixes and decimal prefixes.
Show understanding of binary, denary and hexadecimal number systems, BCD, and one's- and two's-complement representations.
Convert an integer value from one required number base or representation to another.
Perform binary addition and subtraction using positive and negative binary integers.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 2: Communication
coreExplanation: Show understanding of the purpose and benefits of networking devices and the characteristics of LANs and…
Explain client-server and peer-to-peer models, their computer roles, benefits and drawbacks, and justify a model for…
Show understanding of thin-client and thick-client computers and the differences between them.
Show understanding of bus, star, mesh and hybrid network topologies.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 3: Hardware
coreExplanation: Explain the need for input, output, primary storage, secondary storage and removable storage.
Understand embedded systems and their benefits/drawbacks.
Describe principal operation of laser printer, 3D printer, microphone, speakers, HDD, flash memory, optical reader/writer, touchscreen…
Understand why buffers are used.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 4: Processor fundamentals
coreExplanation: Understand Von Neumann architecture and the stored-program concept.
Understand general- and special-purpose registers: PC, MDR, MAR, ACC, IX, CIR and status register.
Understand ALU, CU, clock and immediate access store (IAS).
Understand address, data and control buses.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 5: System software
coreExplanation: Separate the job from the software responsible for it: the OS coordinates resources, utilities perform maintenance or protection tasks, and libraries supply reusable code. Explain the actual operation before claiming a benefit.

Track what is translated, when execution occurs and which environment is required. Match compilation or interpretation to the workload, follow Java through bytecode and the JVM, and use IDE evidence to check behaviour rather than assuming a successful translation proves correctness.

coreExplanation: Distinguish data security, privacy and integrity.
Explain the need for data and computer-system security.
Understand user accounts/passwords, digital signatures, biometrics, firewall, antivirus, anti-spyware and encryption as security measures.
Understand virus, spyware, hackers, phishing and pharming threats.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 7: Ethics and ownership
coreExplanation: Explain why specialists owe duties to affected people, then use the actual decision to identify stakeholders and compare the consequences of ethical and unethical actions. Professional membership supplies standards and development; it leaves the individual responsible for applying them.

For software ownership, distinguish copyright from the permissions in a licence. Compare free-software freedoms, open-source criteria, trial limits and commercial terms against the required use. For AI, describe the task performed before assessing its effects on people, costs and resources.

leadVisual.title: Retrieve and apply the S8 methods

coreExplanation: Start with the information and business rules: identify entities, choose candidate and primary keys, then show relationship cardinalities. Diagnose repeated data and dependency problems before decomposing tables into 3NF. Retain foreign keys that allow the original facts to be reconstructed.

Connect the design to its DBMS implementation. The dictionary describes fields and constraints; access rights and recovery procedures protect use and availability. Read or write DDL to define the structure, and DML to retrieve or maintain records. Trace SQL against the actual data, including join matches, grouped totals and the rows targeted by a maintenance condition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose detail according to the purpose
coreExplanation: Abstraction removes unnecessary detail while retaining the essential features of a problem or system. What counts as essential depends on the purpose: a journey planner needs connections and travel times, whereas a vehicle-painting system may need colours.

A simpler representation reduces the information a designer must consider and makes the important relationships easier to understand. It can also reduce the data and processing needed by the solution. Omitting a detail that changes the required result makes the model unsuitable, even if the model becomes smaller.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Produce and check an abstract model

leadVisual.title: Model for checking a particular copy

coreExplanation: Start by stating what the model must answer. Select the objects, properties and relationships needed for that answer, and represent them with a suitable table or diagram. Record assumptions so the intended limits of the model are clear.

For a library's loan-availability check, a copy identifier and its current loan status can be enough. A title alone cannot distinguish two copies with different availability. Test the representation with one available copy and one borrowed copy before deciding that it captures the required distinction.

objectives.description: Describe and use decomposition
materialTitles: Break down processing a library loan
From a whole task to cooperating parts

objectives.description: Break down problems into sub-problems leading to the concept of a program module (procedure / function)

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate responsibilities

leadVisual.title: Break down processing a library loan

coreExplanation: Decomposition breaks a complex problem into smaller sub-problems. Each part should have a clear responsibility, while the parts together still meet the original requirements. A library loan task can be divided into identifying the copy, checking availability, recording the loan and reporting the result.

Smaller parts are easier to understand, implement and test. Designers can work on separate parts when their interfaces are agreed. A useful breakdown follows the work the system must perform, rather than an arbitrary list of screens or a renamed copy of the whole task.

workedExample.title: From a whole task to cooperating parts

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define module inputs and results
coreExplanation: A program module can implement a sub-problem as a procedure or function. A procedure performs a task when called; a function returns a value that can be used in an expression. Choose responsibilities and interfaces before writing detailed subroutine syntax.

Specify what information each module needs and what result or effect it provides. CalculateCharge can receive a quantity and unit price and return an amount; DisplayReceipt can receive that amount and output it. Repeating the calculation independently in the display module risks disagreement when the charging rule changes.

objectives.description: Use suitable identifier names for the representation of data used by a problem and represent these using an identifier table

materialTitles: Identifiers for reporting a mean mark

knowledgeUnits.heading: Specify an ordered solution
coreExplanation: An algorithm is a solution to a problem expressed as a sequence of defined steps. The order and meaning of the steps must be clear enough to carry out the intended task. Steps may include decisions and repeated actions, so a defined sequence does not mean that every execution follows one straight path.

For a rectangular area, obtain the two dimensions before multiplying them and report the product afterwards. 'Find the area' describes the goal but does not supply the calculation. Conditions also need precise operators: 'at least 18' includes 18 and every greater age, not just the single value 18.

workedExample.title: Turn an area rule into defined operations

knowledgeUnits.heading: Make data names and meanings explicit

leadVisual.title: Identifiers for reporting a mean mark

coreExplanation: An identifier names a data item such as a variable or constant. Select meaningful names that distinguish the item's role, and use each name consistently. MeanMark is more informative than X when the value represents the arithmetic mean of marks.

An identifier table records each name, a suitable data type and its purpose. Whole-number marks can use INTEGER, a mean allowing a fraction needs REAL, and a learner's name needs STRING. The table documents meaning; the program still needs to obtain or calculate values before using them.

objectives.description: Write pseudocode that contains input, process and output
explanationUnits: Identify supplied data and required results
materialTitles: Cost of an order with fixed postage

knowledgeUnits.heading: Identify supplied data and required results

leadVisual.title: Cost of an order with fixed postage

coreExplanation: Input obtains data for the algorithm, processing transforms data or makes decisions, and output communicates a result. Start with the scenario's required output and identify the data and rules needed to produce it. A constant supplied by the problem, such as a fixed postage charge, does not need to be input on every run.

An IPO table is a design aid, not a replacement for the requested pseudocode. Translate each processing rule into an explicit assignment or control structure and show the order in which inputs become available. Include units when a calculation depends on compatible measurements.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write and trace complete statements
coreExplanation: Use INPUT to read into an identifier, an assignment arrow to store an expression's result, and OUTPUT to present values. Cambridge pseudocode uses uppercase keywords and quoted string literals. The left side of an assignment names the destination; the right side is evaluated using the current values.

An output can contain a literal, a variable or an expression. Every variable read by that expression must already have a value. A declaration establishes a type, not an initial value. Trace a concrete case to check the calculation, subtraction order and requested output rather than merely checking that three keywords appear.

objectives.description: Write pseudocode using the three basic constructs of sequence, selection and iteration (repetition)
explanationUnits: Repeat with a defined stopping rule
Place a decision inside a repeated task
materialTitles: A mark selects one of two outcomes
Select a result at an inclusive boundary
Choose a loop from the requirement

knowledgeUnits.heading: Execute dependent operations in order
coreExplanation: Sequence executes instructions in their written order. A later calculation may depend on an earlier input or assignment, so moving operations can change the result or read an unassigned variable. Follow dependencies when placing statements.

For a price calculation, input the quantity before multiplying it by the unit price, then add any fixed charge before outputting the final amount. Declarations can appear first to document types, but they do not perform those calculations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose the correct branch

leadVisual.title: A mark selects one of two outcomes

coreExplanation: Selection chooses operations according to a Boolean condition. In IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF, a true condition selects the THEN block and a false condition selects the ELSE block. Execution continues after ENDIF once the selected block finishes.

Write a condition that matches the exact boundary in the requirement. A pass mark of at least 50 uses Mark >= 50. Mark = 50 would accept only the boundary value and reject higher marks; Mark > 50 would incorrectly reject 50 itself.

workedExample.title: Select a result at an inclusive boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: Repeat with a defined stopping rule

leadVisual.title: Choose a loop from the requirement

coreExplanation: Iteration repeats a block of operations. A FOR loop is suitable when the number of repetitions is known. A WHILE loop tests a condition before the body, so it may execute zero times. A REPEAT ... UNTIL loop tests after the body and therefore executes at least once.

Initialise totals or counts before the loop, update them inside the loop, and put a final aggregate output after the loop. A condition-controlled loop must make progress towards stopping. In a countdown, decreasing Count eventually makes Count > 0 false.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Place a decision inside a repeated task
coreExplanation: The three constructs cooperate in a complete solution. Counting passes begins with an initialisation, repeats input and a decision for each mark, and finishes with one output. Indentation shows that the decision is inside the loop while the final output is outside it.

Read each new mark during its iteration. Increase the count only on the qualifying branch and leave it unchanged otherwise. This arrangement counts qualifying inputs rather than counting all iterations or checking one old input repeatedly.

explanationUnits: Draw a flowchart from a written algorithm
materialTitles: Four inputs contribute to one total

knowledgeUnits.heading: Document a solution in structured English
coreExplanation: Structured English expresses an algorithm using controlled natural-language steps and clear grouping. State the operations in order, identify both outcomes of a decision and make the scope of any repetition explicit. It should leave the same computational choices determined as pseudocode does.

A flowchart shows that control structure with symbols and directed lines, while pseudocode uses statements and indentation. Changing notation should not change the accepted inputs or results. Trace a value on each side of a boundary when comparing two representations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use symbols and arrows consistently
coreExplanation: Use terminators for start and end, parallelograms for input and output, rectangles for processing, and diamonds for decisions. Arrowheads indicate the next operation. Label the outgoing decision paths consistently, for example Yes and No, so the truth value selects an unambiguous route.

A loop needs a return path to its condition or repeated body, according to when it tests. Paths that rejoin must not imply that both selection branches execute. Inspect the arrow direction at the final output as well as at the decision; an output cannot follow an end terminator.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write pseudocode from a flowchart

leadVisual.title: A loop returns to its condition

coreExplanation: Begin at the start symbol and follow the arrows. Translate each input, process and output into its corresponding statement. At a decision, retain the full expression and place each path's operations in the appropriate block. Declare suitable types for the data used by the resulting program.

In the displayed countdown, a false condition goes directly to the final message. A true condition outputs the current value, decreases it and returns to the same test. That control flow corresponds to WHILE, with the message placed after ENDWHILE.

workedExample.title: Recover a loop from directed paths

knowledgeUnits.heading: Draw a flowchart from a written algorithm

leadVisual.title: Four inputs contribute to one total

coreExplanation: When drawing from structured English or pseudocode, identify the sequence, branch boundaries and loop boundaries before choosing symbols. Put a complete condition in every decision and show where execution continues after each path. Convert implicit loop control into visible initialisation, a condition and an update where needed.

A FOR loop that totals four values can be drawn using Index initialised to 1, a decision Index <= 4 and an increment after each addition. The false path outputs the final total. This expands the loop notation while preserving exactly four input operations.

objectives.description: Describe and use the process of stepwise refinement to express an algorithm to a level of detail from which the task may be programmed
materialTitles: Refine one unfinished leaf at a time

knowledgeUnits.heading: Expand the unresolved operations
coreExplanation: Stepwise refinement repeatedly expands an algorithm's high-level steps into more detailed steps. Start with the required result, replace an unresolved operation with a sequence that achieves it, and continue until the remaining actions can be programmed without inventing rules.

Decomposition identifies smaller sub-problems; refinement develops the internal detail of a chosen solution. They can be used together. Refining an average calculation means defining how values are read, how a total is updated and when division occurs, rather than merely naming input, process and output.

method.title: Refine one unfinished leaf at a time

knowledgeUnits.heading: Reach a complete implementation plan
coreExplanation: A useful endpoint states the inputs, initial values, arithmetic, decisions, repetition and outputs required by the task. A programmer should be able to translate the resulting pseudocode directly. The refinement must preserve the original requirement at every level.

Check the final version with concrete data. For three-score averaging, reading all three values and dividing once by three distinguishes the intended mean from a running sum, a last-value calculation or an off-by-one loop. Assumptions about permitted input types and ranges should be stated separately from unfinished operations.

objectives.description: Use logic statements to define parts of an algorithm solution
materialTitles: Truth values of the logical operators

knowledgeUnits.heading: Translate relational boundaries
coreExplanation: A relational expression compares values and produces TRUE or FALSE. Use = for equal, <> for not equal, < and > for strict bounds, and <= or >= when the boundary is included. Read words such as at least, at most, below and above before selecting an operator.

Logical conditions define where an algorithm takes an action or accepts a value. Test the value at the boundary and nearby values on either side. For an integer age requirement of at least 18, 17 must fail while 18 and 19 must pass.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine whole conditions

leadVisual.title: Truth values of the logical operators

coreExplanation: AND is true only when both operands are true. OR is true when either or both operands are true. NOT reverses a Boolean value. Combine complete comparisons and use parentheses to make the intended grouping clear.

Eligibility requiring adulthood and no suspension is (Age >= 18) AND NOT Suspended. A discount available to a child or any member is (Age < 12) OR Member. The English requirement determines the connector; choosing OR where both restrictions are required changes who qualifies.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Test ranges and their complements
coreExplanation: An inclusive range needs the lower and upper comparisons joined by AND. Values outside that range satisfy a below-lower or above-upper test joined by OR. Negating the entire valid-range expression gives the same invalid-range condition.

Use a table of chosen inputs and expected truth values before putting a condition into a larger algorithm. Include both endpoints, one value outside each endpoint and an internal value. For compound eligibility rules, also vary each Boolean input so a missing NOT or wrong connector cannot hide behind one successful example.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decompose the purchase requirements
coreExplanation: This simplified purchase handles one request for identical tickets. Each ticket costs 25.00. Quantity must be at least one and no greater than PlacesLeft. A Boolean Student choice gives 10% off the whole subtotal. After displaying the total, accept payment only when Paid is at least Total; confirm, give change and reduce PlacesLeft only after sufficient payment.

Assume integer Quantity and PlacesLeft, non-negative PlacesLeft and Paid, and correctly typed inputs. Decompose the work into checking quantity, calculating the charge and completing payment. The charge function can return the amount due; a completion procedure can report the outcome and update the available places. The detailed algorithm below expands these responsibilities inline so every operation is visible.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Keep the quantities and amounts consistent
coreExplanation: Derive the purchase calculations from the rules before placing them into pseudocode. Subtotal is the ticket count multiplied by the fixed price. Apply the discount to that subtotal once; Total is either 90% of Subtotal or Subtotal itself. Change subtracts the amount due from the amount paid.

The input path depends on earlier decisions. An unavailable request ends with Unavailable, without asking for a student choice or payment. A valid request obtains Student, calculates and displays Total, and then obtains Paid. Keeping those dependencies explicit prevents using payment or discount data on a path that never reads it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Finish the algorithm and challenge its branches
coreExplanation: Refine check request into two comparisons joined by AND. Refine calculate charge into multiplication followed by a student decision. Refine complete payment into a sufficient-payment comparison with separate success and failure actions. These expansions resolve each high-level responsibility into programmable statements.

Trace successful and rejected cases against the original rules. Zero quantity and requests above availability must exit before charging. Exact payment is sufficient and gives zero change. Underpayment must preserve the available-place count. The final pseudocode provides a complete endpoint, with no placeholder such as process payment left unresolved.
