objectives.description: Recognise ARRAY and FILE in Cambridge pseudocode.
explanationUnits: Recognise ARRAY and FILE in pseudocode

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose a type from the meaning of the value
coreExplanation: INTEGER represents whole numbers; REAL can represent fractional values. CHAR holds one character, whereas STRING holds a sequence of zero or more characters. BOOLEAN has only TRUE and FALSE. DATE represents a valid calendar date. Select a type from the permitted values and required operations, rather than from how a value happens to look.

Cambridge pseudocode declares a variable with DECLARE Identifier : Type. A CHAR literal uses single quotes and a STRING literal uses double quotes. A date is normally written dd/mm/yyyy; state that it is a DATE and specify the format. An assignment stores a value in a declared variable and must be compatible with its type.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Recognise ARRAY and FILE in pseudocode
coreExplanation: An array groups elements of one specified type under a common identifier and selects elements by index. Its declaration gives the bounds and element type. An array is useful when a program needs a fixed set of indexed values during processing.

A file stores data for later use, beyond one execution of a program. The text-file commands in Cambridge pseudocode refer to a file by its name, such as OPENFILE "Names.txt" FOR READ. The quoted file name is a STRING literal identifying a file; it is not a declaration that makes the file's contents a STRING variable.

objectives.description: Explain how a record groups fields of different data types under one identifier.
explanationUnits: Define a record type and declare a variable

objectives.description: Write pseudocode to define a record structure.
explanationUnits: Define a record type and declare a variable

objectives.description: Write pseudocode to read and save data in record fields.
explanationUnits: Read and save values using field names

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define a record type and declare a variable
coreExplanation: A record groups related fields, potentially of different data types, under one identifier. Each field has a name and its own type. A record for one member can therefore hold a STRING name, an INTEGER year group and a BOOLEAN payment state without losing their different meanings.

TYPE MemberRecord introduces the record definition and ENDTYPE closes it. The DECLARE statements inside define its fields. DECLARE Member : MemberRecord then creates a variable of that type; defining the type alone does not create a member or supply values for its fields.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read and save values using field names
coreExplanation: Use dot notation to identify a field, for example Member.YearGroup. INPUT can save a new value directly into that field; an assignment can update it; OUTPUT reads its current value. Updating one field leaves the other fields unchanged.

In the example, the name and current year group are inputs. FeesPaid is explicitly initialised to FALSE, and YearGroup increases by one. Saving data into a record means storing values in its fields. Keeping the record after the program finishes requires a separate file operation.

objectives.description: Use array terminology correctly.
explanationUnits: Distinguish the array, an element and an index

objectives.description: Identify an array's indices and lower and upper bounds.
explanationUnits: Use inclusive lower and upper bounds

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish the array, an element and an index
coreExplanation: An array is a collection of elements of the same data type, stored under one identifier. An index selects a particular element. In Ages[4], Ages names the array and 4 is the index; the value stored in that element might be 17 and is independent of its index.

A one-dimensional array uses one index. A two-dimensional array uses two indices to locate each element. The element type applies to every position, and a declared element must receive a value before an algorithm relies on that value.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use inclusive lower and upper bounds
coreExplanation: The lower bound is the smallest permitted index and the upper bound is the largest. For inclusive bounds L and U, the number of elements is U − L + 1. Cambridge declarations specify these bounds explicitly; an array does not always start at zero or one.

A complete traversal visits each permitted index and stops before exceeding the upper bound. Accessing an out-of-range index is invalid. In two dimensions, both indices must satisfy their own bounds, and capacity is the product of the two dimension lengths.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use one index for one independent position

leadVisual.title: Match a task to a position

coreExplanation: Choose a one-dimensional array when one index identifies each item, such as a test number selecting one mark. The declaration must provide enough positions and an element type suitable for all values. For four whole-number marks, DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:4] OF INTEGER gives one element per test.

An array retains individual values for later indexed access. If a task requires only a running total, a total variable alone may be enough; retaining an array is justified when later processing needs the original marks, for example displaying the third test mark after all inputs have been read.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Input, store and total a 1D array
coreExplanation: Initialise Total once before the traversal. Each iteration inputs a value into Marks[Index], then adds that same element to Total. FOR Index <- 1 TO 4 visits both bounds, and NEXT Index closes the count-controlled loop. No DO keyword is used in this FOR form.

Keeping the final OUTPUT after the loop produces one total for all four elements. OUTPUT Marks[3] then demonstrates that the third value remains available. Moving Total <- 0 inside the loop would discard the contributions from earlier elements.

objectives.description: Write pseudocode to declare and process 1D and 2D arrays.
explanationUnits: Traverse rows with a nested loop
materialTitles: Input six scores and output two row totals

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assign a meaning to each dimension

leadVisual.title: Rows are horizontal; columns are vertical

coreExplanation: Choose a two-dimensional array when two independent positions identify an element. In Scores[Row, Column], let rows represent pupils and columns represent tests. DECLARE Scores : ARRAY[1:2, 1:3] OF INTEGER stores six scores, with the first index selecting the pupil and the second selecting the test.

Rows run horizontally across a displayed table and columns vertically down it. Scores[2,3] is the second pupil's third test score, not the third pupil's second test. State each dimension's meaning before writing code so every reference uses the same convention.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Traverse rows with a nested loop
coreExplanation: The outer loop chooses Row; the inner loop visits every Column for that row. With ascending bounds, the visit order is (1,1), (1,2), (1,3), then (2,1), (2,2), (2,3). The column loop restarts from 1 for each new row, so the second row is not traversed backwards.

RowTotal is reset at the start of each outer iteration because each row needs a separate total. Input and addition occur inside the inner loop, while OUTPUT RowTotal occurs after NEXT Column but before NEXT Row. To calculate column totals, choose a column in the outer loop and vary the row in the inner loop instead.

workedExample.title: Input six scores and output two row totals

objectives.description: Write and trace a bounded linear search.
explanationUnits: Compare each element with the search value

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare each element with the search value
coreExplanation: A linear search checks elements sequentially against a target value. This version searches a 1-based five-element array, reports the first matching index and uses 0 to mean not found. The sentinel is valid because 0 is outside the declared array bounds.

Index begins at the lower bound. A mismatch advances it by one; a match saves the current index in Position. The next loop condition stops once Position is nonzero or Index exceeds 5. Array access occurs inside the guarded loop body, so an unsuccessful search never reads Values[6].

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace found and not-found paths
coreExplanation: The complete algorithm first inputs five values and a target, then initialises the search state. Position starts at 0 for each new search, preventing a previous result from being mistaken for the result of this target. The loop conditions refer only to scalar state; they do not depend on short-circuit evaluation to protect an array subscript.

Test a match at the first position, a match at the final position, an absent target and repeated matching values. An absent target causes five comparisons and finishes with Index equal to 6 and Position still 0. A match at index 5 leaves Position at 5 and performs no sixth comparison.

objectives.description: Write and trace an ascending bubble sort using adjacent comparisons and a complete swap.
explanationUnits: Trace adjacent comparisons and complete passes
Use a swap flag and a shrinking bound
materialTitles: Bubble sort: array after each complete pass
Control state for the diagram input

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace adjacent comparisons and complete passes

leadVisual.title: Bubble sort: array after each complete pass

coreExplanation: An ascending bubble sort compares neighbouring elements from left to right and swaps them if the left value is greater. After the first full pass, the largest value is at the final position. Further passes repeat the process over the remaining unsorted prefix.

Every swap preserves both original values: save the left value in Temp, copy the right value into the left position, then copy Temp into the right position. The diagram records the state after each pass, always with exactly seven elements. Equal adjacent values need no swap.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use a swap flag and a shrinking bound

leadVisual.title: Control state for the diagram input

coreExplanation: Last starts at the upper bound and Swapped starts TRUE so the first pass runs. Reset Swapped to FALSE at the start of each pass and set it TRUE only when a swap occurs. A completed pass with no swaps proves that the remaining adjacent pairs are already ordered.

The inner loop stops at Last − 1 because it also accesses Index + 1. Reducing Last after each pass avoids comparing the sorted suffix again. For the diagram input, pass 3 creates the sorted order; pass 4 makes no swaps and terminates this implementation. Final outputs occur after sorting has finished.

objectives.description: Explain why files are needed.
Write pseudocode to handle text files consisting of one or more lines.
explanationUnits: Read lines with an end-of-file check
Write a new file and append a line

knowledgeUnits.heading: Select the correct file mode
coreExplanation: Files retain data on secondary storage so it can be reused after a program terminates or transferred to another program. Keeping names only in variables or arrays does not provide this persistence. A text file stores a sequence of lines that can be processed in order.

OPENFILE selects how a program will use the named file. READ permits reading existing lines. WRITE creates a file or replaces existing contents. APPEND adds at the end while retaining existing contents. Select the mode from the task: replacing a report and extending a log require different modes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read lines with an end-of-file check
coreExplanation: After OPENFILE in READ mode, check EOF before each READFILE. READFILE copies the next line into a STRING variable and advances the file position. EOF becomes TRUE when there are no further lines to read. CLOSEFILE finishes access after the loop.

A blank line is still a line and can be read as an empty string. It is different from reaching the end of the file. The example outputs and counts every line, including blank ones. For an empty file, the loop body is skipped and the count remains zero.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write a new file and append a line
coreExplanation: WRITEFILE writes the supplied STRING as a line in an open text file. The complete example opens Names.txt FOR WRITE, inputs three lines, writes each line and closes the file. Existing contents are replaced, so this operation suits creating a fresh list.

To extend that list, use APPEND instead. Input a new line, open the same file FOR APPEND, write the line and close the file. Closing completes the file operation and releases the file. When copying between files, use different names so opening the output FOR WRITE cannot erase the input.

objectives.description: Explain that an ADT consists of a collection of data and a set of operations on those data.
explanationUnits: Define the data and operations together
Separate an interface from its implementation
materialTitles: Describe an ADT without choosing storage

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define the data and operations together
coreExplanation: An abstract data type is a collection of data together with a set of operations on those data. The specification describes what each operation does and any conditions for using it. For example, a stack specifies adding at the top and removing the most recently added item.

The word abstract separates observable behaviour from representation. A user of an ADT needs to know which item a removal returns and how empty or full conditions are handled. The user does not need to know the array position or pointer updates that implement the operation.

workedExample.title: Describe an ADT without choosing storage

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate an interface from its implementation
coreExplanation: An implementation chooses concrete storage and procedures that satisfy the ADT's rules. An array implementation may use extra INTEGER variables to track active positions. Those variables are implementation details; changing them must not change the specified order in which clients receive data.

A bounded implementation also needs defined behaviour when storage is full or empty. Rejecting a removal from an empty collection prevents an invalid access. Replacing an array implementation with another representation is acceptable only if valid operations still produce the specified results.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use LIFO for nested or reversible work

leadVisual.title: A stack removes the most recently added item

coreExplanation: A stack is a last-in, first-out structure. PUSH adds an item at the top; POP removes and returns the top item. A peek operation, if provided, reads the top item without removing it. Items below the top wait until the items above them have been removed.

Undo history and nested subroutine calls fit this access order. The latest action is undone first, and the most recent unfinished call returns before an earlier call resumes. Choose a stack because of that ordering requirement, rather than merely because the task stores several items.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Track the active top in an array

leadVisual.title: Capacity 3; Top identifies the last occupied cell

coreExplanation: In this 1-based array model, Top is the index of the last occupied element; Top = 0 means empty. To push, check that Top is below capacity, increase Top and store the new item at that position. To pop, check that Top is above zero, read the top value and decrease Top.

Editing the top item changes its stored value without changing Top. Access to a deeper item must follow the permitted interface, for example temporarily popping the items above it and restoring them in reverse removal order. Removing an item does not require erasing its old cell; positions above Top are inactive.

explanationUnits: Add at the rear and remove from the front

explanationUnits: Use front, rear and count consistently

knowledgeUnits.heading: Add at the rear and remove from the front
coreExplanation: A queue is a first-in, first-out structure. ENQUEUE adds at the rear and DEQUEUE removes and returns the front item. A new arrival joins behind the items already waiting, so serving the front preserves arrival order.

A first-come, first-served print queue or service desk suits FIFO. The requirement concerns waiting items: a job already removed is no longer in the queue. An ordinary FIFO queue does not automatically move a later urgent job ahead of earlier arrivals; that would require different scheduling rules.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use front, rear and count consistently

leadVisual.title: A queue removes the earliest item still waiting

coreExplanation: This circular array implementation uses Front for the next removal position, Rear for the last occupied insertion position, and Count for the number of active items. Initially Front = 1, Rear = 0 and Count = 0. A successful enqueue advances Rear with wrap-around, stores the item and increases Count; a dequeue reads Front, advances it with wrap-around and decreases Count.

Count = 0 means empty and Count = capacity means full. Wrapping from the final index back to 1 reuses positions released by earlier dequeues. An allowed edit changes an active item's value without changing its arrival position or Count. Reading or editing an inactive cell must not turn it into a waiting item.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Represent a sequence using nodes and links

leadVisual.title: Follow links, not consecutive array positions

coreExplanation: A linked list contains nodes, each holding data and a link to the next node. A head pointer identifies the first node. In the model used here, a link value of 0 means no next node; Head = 0 represents an empty list. The last active node has a null link.

Logical order is determined by links, not by consecutive storage positions. Follow the head and successive links to traverse the list. A linked list suits a sequence that needs insertions or deletions between neighbours because changing links can avoid shifting every following data item, although locating the required node may still require traversal.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Update data and links without losing nodes

leadVisual.title: Operations on the starting A → B → C list

coreExplanation: An array implementation can store Data[Index] and Next[Index] for each node, plus Head and information about unused slots. To insert X at free slot 3 after node 2 in the diagram, first store X and set Next[3] to the old successor 4. Then set Next[2] to 3. The sequence becomes A, X, B, C.

Editing a node's data leaves its links unchanged. Deleting a middle node makes its predecessor point to the deleted node's successor, then returns the removed slot to the available storage. Deleting the head updates Head instead. The programmer must preserve access to the successor before changing links, or the remaining chain can become unreachable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Check active positions when an array is reused

leadVisual.title: Capacity 4; old cell values are not membership

coreExplanation: An array-backed stack and queue can contain inactive cells whose old values are still visible in memory. For a stack with Top as the last occupied index, only positions 1 through Top are active. For a circular queue, Count active positions begin at Front and wrap through the array; Rear identifies the last one when Count is positive.

Check representation state before adding, editing or deleting. A full structure cannot accept another item without a specified capacity change; an empty structure cannot supply an item. Value edits preserve membership and order, whereas push/pop or enqueue/dequeue change membership and must update the corresponding state variables.

workedExample.title: Check an edit against active membership

knowledgeUnits.heading: Track free nodes separately from the active list
coreExplanation: A fixed array implementation of a linked list needs a way to find unused nodes. One method links unused positions into a free list with its own Free head pointer. Active and free chains must not share nodes. A null Free pointer means the array has no available slot for another insertion.

To allocate a node, take the position identified by Free and advance Free to that node's old free link before reusing the link for the active chain. To release a deleted node, remove it from the active chain first, link it to the current free head and make it the new Free head. This reuses storage without shifting surviving node data.

coreExplanation: Separate the values the application must retain from the order in which it processes actions. A theatre can store one occupancy flag per row and seat in a 2D BOOLEAN array. A separate 1D INTEGER array can store one booking total per performance, because performance number alone identifies each total.

Describe the meaning and bounds of each dimension explicitly. Occupied[Row, Seat] uses two indices; Bookings[Performance] uses one. The declaration should follow the data's actual indexing needs. Adding dimensions simply because a system is large creates an unnecessary or misleading model.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Justify each ADT by its operation order
coreExplanation: The same theatre can use a queue for booking requests processed in arrival order and a stack for reversing the most recent completed edits. A linked list can represent a running order of acts that frequently receives insertions between known neighbours. Each choice follows a specific access or update requirement.

Explain how the structures cooperate: dequeue a request, use its row and seat to access the occupancy array, and push an undo record containing the previous state after a successful change. The request queue and undo stack contain different items and have different removal orders. Merely naming all three ADTs does not justify a design.

objectives.description: Implement and write pseudocode from a given design presented as either a program flowchart or structured English
materialTitles: Flowchart: count positives in three inputs

knowledgeUnits.heading: Translate structured English
coreExplanation: Read the whole design before writing statements. Identify the inputs, initial values, processing order and required outputs. Translate a precise action such as increase Count by one into Count <- Count + 1; do not leave the action as an unexplained instruction to process data.

Consider this design: set a count to zero; read three integers in turn; increase the count for each positive integer; output the final count. Initialisation belongs before repetition, the input and positive-value decision belong inside it, and the final output belongs after it. Indentation makes these responsibilities visible.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow every flowchart edge

leadVisual.title: Flowchart: count positives in three inputs

coreExplanation: A flowchart's arrows specify execution order. A decision requires both outcomes to reach the correct next operation. A backward arrow identifies repetition; determine which state changes before execution returns to the decision. A terminal marks the end of that execution path.

The flowchart below implements the same three-value design. Count and Index are initialised before the first test. Each completed input advances Index once, including a non-positive value. The loop exits to the final output when Index exceeds three; execution ends after that output.

objectives.description: Declare and initialise constants.
Declare variables with Cambridge data types.
Assign expression values to variables.
Read keyboard input and write console output.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare variables and constants
coreExplanation: Use DECLARE Identifier : DataType for a variable. Choose INTEGER for whole-number counts, REAL for values that may have a fractional part, BOOLEAN for TRUE or FALSE, CHAR for one character and STRING for text. A declaration does not provide an initial value.

Declare and initialise a named constant with CONSTANT Identifier = Literal. Its type follows from the literal and its value remains fixed. Use double quotes for a STRING literal and single quotes for a CHAR literal. In this notation a constant declaration uses a literal, rather than an expression involving other identifiers.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Obtain, assign and output values
coreExplanation: Assignment evaluates the expression on the right and stores the result in the variable on the left. Total <- Price * Quantity changes Total; Total = Price * Quantity is a comparison. A later assignment replaces the variable's earlier value. INPUT obtains a value from the keyboard, while OUTPUT writes a value or expression to the console.

For a purchase with tax charged per item, read Price and Quantity before using either. Compute Tax <- Price * TaxRate, then multiply the tax-inclusive item price by Quantity. Declaring all identifiers, obtaining the inputs and assigning intermediate results in order prevents undefined values from reaching the calculation.

objectives.description: Assign expression values to variables.
Use arithmetic and logical operators in expressions.
materialTitles: Test both sides of the rule
Convert minutes and test a permitted interval

knowledgeUnits.heading: Evaluate arithmetic and integer division
coreExplanation: Arithmetic expressions use +, -, * and /. Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction; parentheses override that order. The / operator produces a real division result even when both operands are integers. Choose a REAL destination when a fractional result is possible.

DIV gives the integer quotient and MOD gives the remainder. For a non-negative number of minutes, Minutes DIV 60 gives complete hours and Minutes MOD 60 gives minutes left over. The divisor must be non-zero. Parentheses are useful when an expression combines arithmetic operations with a comparison.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build and test Boolean expressions

leadVisual.title: Test both sides of the rule

coreExplanation: Comparisons =, <>, <, <=, > and >= produce Boolean values. AND requires both conditions to be true; OR is true when either or both are true; NOT reverses a Boolean value. Write each comparison in full, including the identifier on both sides of an interval test.

An adult threshold uses Age >= 18, which accepts 18 and every greater age. An inclusive interval from zero to 180 uses (Minutes >= 0) AND (Minutes <= 180). Test both endpoints and outside values. Its complement uses (Minutes < 0) OR (Minutes > 180); replacing AND by OR without changing the comparisons admits every value.

objectives.description: Apply the supplied definitions of string manipulation functions.
explanationUnits: Apply supplied string and character interfaces

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use numeric built-in functions
coreExplanation: A built-in function is supplied by the language; a library routine supplies reusable operations through an interface. A function call gives arguments in the specified order and supplies a returned value to the surrounding expression. Check the accepted types and the meaning of the result before using it.

INT(X) returns the integer part of real X. RAND(X), for a positive integer bound X, returns a real value from zero inclusive to X exclusive. INT(RAND(6)) + 1 therefore produces an integer from one to six. The addition shifts the possible values after truncation; RAND(6) alone does not return a die face.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Apply supplied string and character interfaces
coreExplanation: In examinations, string manipulation functions are supplied; other functions absent from the pseudocode guide are also defined. Read those definitions rather than assuming that a familiar name uses another language's indexing or argument order. The table here supplies the contracts needed for the lesson's examples.

LENGTH(Text) returns a string's character count; MID(Text, Start, Count) takes Count characters beginning at the one-based Start position; RIGHT(Text, Count) takes the rightmost characters. UCASE and LCASE here accept and return a single CHAR. Supply indices and counts valid for the stated string; the examples do not rely on unspecified out-of-range behaviour.

objectives.description: Write IF, ELSE and nested IF statements.
Write a CASE structure.
explanationUnits: Select by the value of one identifier

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write alternatives and nested decisions
coreExplanation: An IF statement executes its THEN block when the condition is true. An optional ELSE block handles the false outcome. ENDIF closes that decision. Two independent IF statements can both execute their blocks; IF with ELSE selects only one of its alternatives.

Nesting puts a second decision inside a branch of the first. For adult membership, check Age >= 18 first and check Member only inside the adult branch. Give each IF its own ENDIF and indent consistently so the reader can identify which ELSE belongs to which decision.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Select by the value of one identifier
coreExplanation: Use CASE OF Identifier when alternatives depend on the value of one identifier. Put each value or permitted range before a colon, provide its statements, and close the structure with ENDCASE. OTHERWISE handles a value that matches no listed case; no break statement is needed in Cambridge pseudocode.

For a menu, Choice 1 opens and Choice 2 saves; every other value reports Invalid. This is clearer than a long series of equality tests on Choice. Use IF for general Boolean conditions or nested rules involving different data, and ensure CASE labels express distinct intended alternatives.

objectives.description: Write a count-controlled FOR loop.
explanationUnits: Use an explicit step and direction
materialTitles: Total a specified number of integers

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use inclusive count-controlled bounds
coreExplanation: A FOR loop is suitable when the iteration count is known before entering the loop. Write FOR Index <- Start TO End and close it with NEXT Index. With the default step of one, the body uses Start, Start + 1 and so on up to End inclusive. Let the loop manage its control variable.

FOR Index <- 1 TO Count performs Count iterations for a non-negative Count. Count zero gives no iterations, and Count one gives exactly one. Initialise an accumulator before the loop; obtain each new value and add it inside; report the total afterwards. A zero-item total remains the initial zero without a special loop branch.

workedExample.title: Total a specified number of integers

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use an explicit step and direction
coreExplanation: STEP supplies the integer increment instead of the default one. A positive step moves upward; a negative step moves downward. The body runs while the control value remains within the endpoint in that direction. The endpoint is used only if the sequence of increments reaches it exactly.

FOR Index <- 6 TO 0 STEP -2 visits 6, 4, 2 and 0. Starting at 5 with the same endpoint and step visits 5, 3 and 1, then stops before -1. A step of zero makes no progress and is unsuitable. Choose the starting value, endpoint and direction together before counting executions.

objectives.description: Write a post-condition REPEAT loop.
materialTitles: Read a mark in the inclusive range

objectives.description: Write a pre-condition WHILE loop.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use a post-condition REPEAT loop
coreExplanation: A post-condition loop tests after the body, so its statements execute at least once. Write REPEAT, the body, then UNTIL Condition. A true condition stops repetition; a false condition sends execution back to the body. There is no ENDREPEAT in this syntax.

Input validation commonly needs a first attempt before it can judge the value. Read Mark inside REPEAT and stop when (Mark >= 0) AND (Mark <= 100). Each invalid integer triggers another input. This example assumes correctly typed integers: checking a numeric range does not itself handle text entered in place of a number.

workedExample.title: Read a mark in the inclusive range

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use a pre-condition WHILE loop
coreExplanation: A pre-condition loop tests before the body, which may run zero times. Write WHILE Condition, the indented body and ENDWHILE; Cambridge pseudocode does not add DO to the WHILE header. TRUE continues into the body and FALSE skips to the next statement after ENDWHILE.

For a sentinel-controlled total, read Value before the first test so the condition has a defined value. While Value <> -1, add the value and read the next one. The sentinel -1 ends input and is not included in the total. A sentinel entered first gives an empty data set and total zero.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare test position and polarity
coreExplanation: Test position and condition meaning are separate choices. WHILE Valid continues when Valid is true, whereas UNTIL Valid stops when Valid is true. Moving the same condition from one loop header to the other without considering its meaning can reverse the algorithm's behaviour.

A translation between loop forms must also preserve the first-iteration rule. Replacing a WHILE loop directly with REPEAT forces an execution even when the original pre-condition was false. Establish the allowed input assumptions and, where necessary, use an outer decision to retain the original zero-iteration path.

objectives.description: Justify why one loop structure may be better suited to solve a problem than the others
explanationUnits: Combine a condition with a maximum attempt count
materialTitles: Stop on success or the attempt limit

knowledgeUnits.heading: Justify from the problem's conditions
coreExplanation: A loop justification connects a property of the problem to a property of the chosen structure. Use FOR when the count is known before repetition. Use REPEAT when an action must happen before its result can be checked. Use WHILE when the continuation rule can be checked before processing and no body execution may be needed.

Different loop structures can often implement the same result with additional setup. Explain suitability rather than claiming that alternatives are impossible or inherently slower. For twelve readings a count-controlled header exposes the count; for repeated menu input a post-condition loop places the first request before validation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine a condition with a maximum attempt count
coreExplanation: Some repetitions end for either of two reasons. A password attempt sequence stops on success or after three attempts. Initialise Password and Attempts before WHILE, then continue only while the password is wrong AND fewer than three attempts have occurred. Increment the counter after every input, including a successful attempt.

A WHILE loop states the combined continuation rule directly and can be adapted when a preliminary condition should prevent attempts. A REPEAT loop could also express the task if at least one attempt is required, using an UNTIL condition for success OR three attempts. A fixed three-iteration FOR without an extra guard would continue asking after early success.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define and call procedures
coreExplanation: A procedure groups statements that perform an action. Use it for a responsibility such as displaying a heading or updating a total when no function result is required in an expression. Define it with PROCEDURE Name(parameters) and ENDPROCEDURE; invoke it with CALL Name(arguments). A definition alone does not execute the body.

A procedure can take no parameters, one parameter or several parameters. Heading() needs none, Show(Value) receives one value, and Add(Total, Amount) receives two. State each formal parameter's type and preserve the declared order at the call. Empty parentheses remain in a no-parameter definition and call.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace parameter passing
coreExplanation: BYVAL passes a copy of an argument's value; it is the default parameter mode when no mode is specified. Changing this local parameter leaves the caller's scalar variable unchanged. A value argument may be an appropriate literal or expression, because only its evaluated value is needed.

BYREF makes the parameter refer to the caller's variable, so an assignment through the parameter changes that variable. Pass an assignable variable of the required type, not a literal such as 5 or a temporary expression. Use reference passing only for data that the procedure is intended to update, and trace both the local view and caller state.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define and use a returned value
coreExplanation: A function is a subprogram that returns a value. Its header uses FUNCTION Name(parameters) RETURNS DataType and its body uses RETURN Expression, ending with ENDFUNCTION. The returned expression must match the declared result type, and every reachable result path must supply a return value.

Call a function where its result is needed: in an assignment, condition, output or another expression. Total <- Price + Tax(Price) adds the returned tax to the original price. Do not prefix a function call with CALL; that keyword invokes a procedure. Function parameters use value passing in this Cambridge notation.

workedExample.title: Use a function result in a calculation

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read headers, parameters and arguments
coreExplanation: A subprogram interface describes how it can be called: its name, ordered formal parameters, their types and relevant passing modes, plus the result type for a function. The header records these details. A caller should be able to use the interface without depending on the internal calculation steps.

A parameter is the identifier declared in the subprogram header. An argument is the value, variable or expression supplied at a call. In ValidMark(Value), Mark is the formal parameter and Value is the argument; the result is a BOOLEAN. A correct interface also needs a clear behavioural contract, such as accepting marks from zero to 100 inclusive.

objectives.description: Write efficient pseudocode

knowledgeUnits.heading: Identify repeated work
coreExplanation: Efficient pseudocode avoids unnecessary operations while remaining correct and understandable. Look for repeated calculations, repeated tests with unchanged operands and avoidable traversals. Meaningful identifiers and indentation support review, but a shorter line count alone does not establish fewer operations.

In the example, Mark is read once and is not changed between two identical Mark >= 50 tests. The first test increments Count and the second displays Pass. Both operations can share one true branch. This reduces two comparisons to one for every run while retaining the action order and final count.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Refactor and check behavioural equivalence
coreExplanation: Move both pass-only actions inside one IF Mark >= 50 block, keeping Count's initialisation before the decision and OUTPUT Count afterwards. A failed mark then skips both actions, just as in the original. A passing mark increments before displaying Pass, preserving the observable sequence.

Compare original and revised versions for below-boundary, boundary and above-boundary inputs. Check outputs and updated values, not merely whether execution finishes. Reusable functions can also centralise a rule such as ValidMark, but a function call is not automatically a speed improvement; measure the operation or duplication that the change actually removes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Turn the complete design into responsibilities
coreExplanation: Implement this structured English: initialise Total and Passed to zero; obtain three valid integer marks, accepting the interval zero to 100 inclusive; for each accepted mark add it to Total and increase Passed when it is at least 50; finally output the mean and pass count. Incorrectly typed inputs are outside this task's assumptions.

Separate deciding validity from updating the accumulated results. The main program controls the number of accepted marks, the validation function answers a Boolean question, and the recording procedure performs the updates. All three parts must use the same interval, threshold and accepted-mark count.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Nest validation inside the known count
coreExplanation: Use a FOR loop for the three accepted-mark slots. Inside each iteration, use REPEAT to obtain at least one attempt and UNTIL ValidMark(Mark) to finish validation. Only then call RecordMark. The nested input loop may repeat many times while the outer loop still advances once per accepted mark.

The pass comparison belongs to the recording action after validation. With inputs -1, 0, 50, 101, 100, the accepted values are 0, 50 and 100. Their sum is 150, their mean is 50 and two satisfy the inclusive pass threshold. Output the mean and count after all accepted marks have been recorded.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Connect the subprograms and verify the result
coreExplanation: ValidMark takes its INTEGER argument by value and returns a BOOLEAN used by UNTIL. RecordMark receives Mark by value, because it only reads that mark, and Total and Passed by reference, because it must update the caller's accumulators. The order at CALL RecordMark(Mark, Total, Passed) matches the header.

Read the complete program from definitions through initialisation, repetition and final output. Test all failing marks, all passing marks and rejected attempts followed by valid boundaries. A correct return condition is (Mark >= 0) AND (Mark <= 100); using equality at zero would reject every other valid mark.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Purpose and stages of a development life cycle

leadVisual.title: A library renewal feature through five stages

coreExplanation: A development life cycle organises the work needed to produce and support a program. It gives the team an agreed route from understanding the problem to a tested solution, with records that connect requirements, design decisions and results. A model helps coordinate responsibilities and review progress; following a list of stages alone does not guarantee a suitable product.

Analysis establishes the problem, user requirements and constraints. Design specifies the solution, including data, algorithms, module interfaces and tests. Coding implements the design. Testing compares actual behaviour with expected results and exposes defects. Maintenance changes the delivered program as faults, environments and user needs change. Feedback can reveal a need to revisit earlier work.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Waterfall: planned sequential stages
coreExplanation: Waterfall completes planned stages largely in sequence. The output of one stage is reviewed before the next proceeds, so requirements and designs provide a documented basis for implementation and testing. It is useful where requirements are well understood and stable and formal approval records are valuable.

The staged structure makes milestones and responsibilities clear. However, users may see working software late, and a requirement change discovered after design or coding can force substantial rework. Returning to earlier work is possible; it undermines the assumption that the earlier stage was settled.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Iterative development: learn from successive versions
coreExplanation: Iterative development revisits analysis, design, coding and testing through successive versions. An early version is reviewed, and the findings guide the next cycle. This allows feedback to refine a solution when the team does not yet understand every requirement.

Users can evaluate working behaviour before the whole system is finished, reducing the risk of building the wrong solution. Repeated changes also need scope, version and schedule control: without clear priorities and stopping criteria, additional cycles can delay completion and make documentation inconsistent.

knowledgeUnits.heading: RAD and choosing a suitable model
coreExplanation: Rapid application development (RAD) emphasises rapid prototyping, time-boxed development and frequent user involvement. Users inspect early working prototypes and give prompt feedback that changes the next version. Short agreed development periods concentrate effort on a usable result rather than waiting for every feature.

RAD can suit an interactive booking interface when users are available and components can be prototyped quickly. Limited user availability or tightly dependent components can make this approach difficult. A project needing exhaustive assurance and stable approved documentation may find rapid changes harder to control. Choose a model by relating these features to requirement stability, delivery time, user access and assurance needs.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decompose a problem into a structure chart
coreExplanation: A structure chart records the decomposition of a problem into modules. A rectangle names a module, and a connecting hierarchy line shows a calling relationship. Place the controlling module above the modules it calls, then refine a large subtask into another level when needed. The chart documents the overall design rather than every statement executed inside a module.

For one order, ProcessOrder obtains a positive integer Quantity and a non-negative real UnitPrice, calculates their product and displays the cost. The three child modules have distinct responsibilities. ReadOrder obtains the inputs, CalculateCost returns their product, and DisplayCost presents the supplied amount. For this example the parent calls them in that left-to-right sequence.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Make parameters and returned values explicit
coreExplanation: Label each transferred value and show its direction. A module needs an input value before it can use that value. ReadOrder instead supplies newly entered values back to the parent, so its parameters are passed by reference. CalculateCost can receive copies of the quantity and price by value and return one numeric cost.

A formal parameter appears in a procedure or function header. An argument appears in the call. The number, order and types must match the interface. A function result is assigned or used in an expression; a procedure that changes a by-reference argument can update the caller's variable without returning a function value.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Derive and check equivalent pseudocode
coreExplanation: Convert module boxes into complete subprogram definitions with the specified interfaces. Inside each parent, write calls or function expressions in the required order. Add the module bodies from the problem requirements; a chart gives responsibility and interface information but does not supply every internal statement.

Check equivalence by following the same data through chart and program. In this design, the reader changes the parent's two variables, the function computes their product, and the display procedure receives that result. Declarations, parameter modes, return type and argument order must agree. A list of headers without the parent calls or bodies is not a complete implementation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Document persistent states and transitions

leadVisual.title: A turnstile has two persistent states

coreExplanation: A state-transition diagram documents the possible conditions of a system and the events that move it between those conditions. It helps a designer communicate behaviour that depends on the current state. An initial-state indicator tells the reader where an event sequence starts.

In the turnstile model, a coin unlocks a locked barrier and passing locks it again. A push while locked leaves it locked. A second coin while already unlocked leaves it unlocked. Each arrow is directed and labelled with an event; a self-loop represents an event that leaves the current state unchanged. More detailed diagrams may add conditions to an event label.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace behaviour and distinguish design documents
coreExplanation: Read one event at a time, starting at the initial state. Follow an outgoing arrow whose label matches that event and any stated condition, then use the new state for the next event. An arrow from another state cannot be used merely because its label matches.

A structure chart answers which modules call other modules; a state-transition diagram answers which state changes are possible. A flowchart records processing steps and control flow. These documents can describe different aspects of one system, but none should be read as a substitute for the others. If a required event has no transition from the current state, the diagram needs clarification rather than an invented transition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish errors and reduce their likelihood
coreExplanation: A syntax error breaks the grammar of the language, such as an IF statement without its required ENDIF. A translator or syntax checker can report it. A logic error uses accepted syntax but implements the wrong requirement; execution may finish with an incorrect result. A run-time error occurs during execution, for example an attempted division by zero or opening a file that is not available.

Clear requirements, modular design, meaningful identifiers, consistent indentation and review help avoid faults. Validate input where required, check preconditions before risky operations and use complete constructs. These practices reduce risk but do not prove a program fault-free. Tests, traces and diagnostics provide evidence about particular behaviours.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Expose a failure and locate its cause
coreExplanation: Begin with a specific input, an expected result derived from the requirement and the actual result. Reproduce the mismatch, then narrow the search using translator messages, a manual trace or debugger evidence. A diagnostic line may be where the failure becomes visible rather than where the incorrect value originated.

For a pass rule of at least 50, trace the complete selection with Mark equal to 50. In the supplied faulty program, Mark > 50 evaluates to FALSE and the ELSE branch assigns Fail. This identifies the comparison as the cause. A condition Mark < 50 is not inherently faulty: it would be correct for a Fail branch with a Pass alternative.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Correct the cause, then retest
coreExplanation: Make a correction that follows from the diagnosed cause. For the faulty Pass branch, change the comparison to Mark >= 50. Repeat the failing case to demonstrate the correction, then run relevant existing tests to check that previously correct behaviour still works. This second purpose is regression testing.

A run-time failure also needs a defined response, not just a change that suppresses the symptom. If there are no values to average, a Count greater than zero guard prevents division by zero and the alternative can output No data. State that zero-count behaviour in the requirement and verify it along with an ordinary nonzero case.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Dry runs and walkthroughs
coreExplanation: A dry run manually follows an algorithm with selected input data. Record changing variables, decisions and output in a trace table; use the actual statements, including initialisation and loop limits. This can expose logic faults without running the program on a computer.

A walkthrough is a structured review in which the author explains the design or code to others. Participants follow representative cases, question assumptions and record faults or omissions. A walkthrough can include a manual trace, but the collaborative discussion is distinct from a person carrying out a dry run alone.

knowledgeUnits.heading: White-box and black-box test design

leadVisual.title: Two reasons to choose a case

coreExplanation: White-box testing uses knowledge of the internal code structure to choose test cases, for example inputs that make a decision true and false. Coverage evidence records which branches or paths have executed. Exercising every branch is useful but does not prove that every requirement was implemented.

Black-box testing derives inputs and expected outputs from the specification without relying on the internal algorithm. For a 10% member discount, tests should distinguish a member from a non-member and compare the amount due with the specified calculation. Both approaches can use the same input values; what differs is the reason for selecting them.

workedExample.title: Select cases for a price decision

knowledgeUnits.heading: Integration testing and stubs

leadVisual.title: Booking caller with an availability stub

coreExplanation: Integration testing checks modules working together, especially their interfaces: argument types, order, returned values and the meaning of transferred data. Individually correct modules can still fail when one supplies metres and another expects centimetres, or when a result is passed to the wrong parameter.

A stub temporarily replaces a called module that is not yet available. It can return a controlled value so the caller and available interfaces can be exercised. Record what the stub simulates and replace it with the real module for further integration tests; a passing stub-based test does not verify the absent module's implementation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Alpha, beta and acceptance testing

leadVisual.title: Choose the method for the purpose

coreExplanation: Alpha testing takes place under developer control before wider release, using internal testers and sometimes user representatives to expose faults in a controlled setting. Beta testing gives a near-complete version to selected external users in their own realistic environments, where different devices and usage patterns can reveal additional problems.

Acceptance testing checks the delivered system against agreed user requirements so the customer can decide whether to accept it. Select cases that demonstrate those requirements, rather than treating all user feedback as acceptance evidence. Beta feedback can be broad and uneven, while acceptance checks need explicit pass conditions linked to the agreed system.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Plan the overall testing approach

leadVisual.title: An outline strategy for room bookings

coreExplanation: A test strategy sets the overall approach: what will be tested, which levels and methods will be used, the sequence of work, responsibilities, resources and conditions for starting or finishing a phase. It helps a team coordinate testing and decide how the evidence will address project risks and requirements.

For a room-booking program, individual module checks can precede integration tests of the availability and booking modules. Customer acceptance can then use agreed booking rules. Naming a method alone is insufficient planning: identify who performs it, what environment or data it needs, and what results allow work to proceed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Record cases and compare outcomes

leadVisual.title: Room capacity is 30; Quantity is an integer

coreExplanation: A test plan records the cases to run, with identifiers, purposes, input data or initial conditions and expected results. Expected results are decided from the specification before execution. The plan can then record actual results and a pass/fail decision, with defect and retest records where needed.

Give enough detail for another tester to repeat the case. For a room limited to 30 people, a request of 31 should be rejected; an actual acceptance is a failure even if the program runs without an error message. When corrected, preserve the original failure record and record the new run so the evidence shows what changed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish ordinary, invalid and extreme values
coreExplanation: Normal test data are valid values representative of ordinary use. Abnormal data violate a stated rule, such as a range, type or format restriction, and should receive the specified rejection or error response. Extreme values are the valid endpoints of an accepted range.

Boundary testing examines a limit and useful values immediately on either side. State explicitly whether each chosen value is valid or invalid: for an integer range 0 to 100, 0 and 100 are valid extremes, while -1 and 101 are abnormal values just outside. The term boundary describes their position relative to the limit and must not hide their expected acceptance or rejection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Select cases that distinguish likely faults
coreExplanation: First identify the rule, data type, limits and inclusive or exclusive comparisons. Choose a normal case, values exactly at each limit and values just outside. Where useful, include values just inside so an incorrect narrow equality test is exposed. Supply the expected result of each case, not just a label such as boundary.

For a username length from 6 to 12 inclusive, lengths 5 and 13 must be rejected, while 6 and 12 must be accepted. Strings with these lengths are actual test data; the word short is not. For real-valued measurements, select nearby values at the precision permitted by the specification rather than assuming that one whole unit is the next value.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why maintenance continues after delivery
coreExplanation: Maintenance keeps a delivered system useful as its circumstances change. Real use can expose faults missed by pre-release tests. New operating systems, equipment, regulations or external interfaces may require adaptation. Users may also need additional features or better performance after the original requirements have been met.

A requested change should be understood before editing. Identify affected modules, data and interfaces, then check the revised behaviour and relevant existing functions. Keep the request, change and test evidence connected so later maintainers can understand why the system behaves as it does.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Classify by the reason for the change

leadVisual.title: Three changes to one report module

coreExplanation: Corrective maintenance repairs faults in the delivered system, such as a receipt showing a total that violates its existing calculation rule. Adaptive maintenance responds to a changed operating environment or external requirement, such as a new operating-system interface or revised legal rule.

Perfective maintenance improves functionality, performance or usability, such as adding requested export options or speeding up a search. The edited file does not determine the category: the same reporting module could receive all three kinds of change on different occasions. Explain the cause given in the scenario rather than classifying every alteration as corrective.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Analyse the supplied program before changing it

leadVisual.title: Impact of the new merit requirement

coreExplanation: Read the existing program and state its purpose, inputs, outputs, data and control flow. Identify assumptions and trace representative inputs so you know what the current result means. Then compare the new requirement with that behaviour to locate where extra data or processing belongs.

The supplied program reads four already validated integer marks from 0 to 100 and counts those at least 50. PassCount is initialised once before the loop, updated inside the selection and output after all four inputs. The requested enhancement is to output an additional MeritCount for marks at least 70 while preserving the original pass count.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Amend all affected parts coherently
coreExplanation: Add the declaration, initialisation, update and output needed for the new feature. The merit condition belongs inside the same traversal, after each Mark is obtained. A mark of 70 qualifies for both counts, so use two independent selections; an ELSE branch between them would make the categories mutually exclusive.

Keep the old pass comparison and output unless the request explicitly changes them. A focused amendment is easier to explain and test than an unrelated rewrite. The complete amended program below allows both counts to be compared with the original behaviour for the same input sequence.

workedExample.title: Add merit counting without losing passes

knowledgeUnits.heading: Test the enhancement and check for regressions
coreExplanation: Test the new decision with values that exercise its boundary and both outcomes. Also repeat cases that protect the original decision. For this example 69 and 70 distinguish the merit threshold, while 49 and 50 protect the pass threshold. Compute both expected counts before executing the amended program.

Test collections of inputs as well as one isolated value. All marks below 50 must leave both counters zero; four merit marks must increment both counters four times. Such cases expose misplaced initialisation, missing increments and incorrect mutual exclusion. Record the amended outputs alongside the original output so preservation is explicit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 9: Algorithm design and problem-solving
coreExplanation: Begin with the required result and retain the facts that determine it. Decompose the task into cooperating responsibilities, choose meaningful identifiers and refine the processing until the rules and execution order are explicit. The resulting IPO, pseudocode and flowchart should describe the same solution.

Challenge a completed algorithm at decision boundaries and loop limits. Follow each path using actual values, checking initialisation, new inputs, updates and the final output. A convincing design combines correct logic with a representation that another programmer can implement without guessing.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 10: Data types and structures
coreExplanation: Choose each value's type before grouping values: record fields may have different types, whereas an array has a declared element type and explicit bounds. One index selects a 1D element; two select a 2D element. Write complete declarations, field access and bounded iteration before tracing the resulting values.

For array processing, linear search checks consecutive elements and reports a matching position or absence; bubble sort uses complete adjacent swaps. Files retain results between runs through the appropriate read, write or append mode. ADTs specify data and operations: use LIFO for a stack, FIFO for a queue and links for a linked list, and keep the array implementation's active state consistent after each operation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 11: Programming
coreExplanation: Translate the stated rules into declarations, expressions and correctly placed control structures. Read supplied routine interfaces before calling them. A complete solution defines values before use, respects condition boundaries and makes progress toward the stopping condition.

Connect subprograms through arguments, returned values and intentional reference updates. In this review, a parking session costs 3 per whole hour; positive integer hours are entered until sentinel zero. A charge function returns each fee and an accumulation procedure updates the running total. The first input may already be zero.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 12: Software development
coreExplanation: Connect each development decision to observable evidence: requirements and project constraints guide the life cycle; a hierarchy and labelled interfaces guide implementation; states and transitions document event-dependent behaviour. Use a trace to check that the resulting algorithm implements the intended rules.

Choose tests for the risks being examined and record their expected results before running them. After delivery, identify why a change is needed, analyse its impact, make the requested amendment and check both changed and preserved behaviour. A category name alone cannot demonstrate any of these practical skills.
